Term: How many interleavings do 2 threads with k statements each have?
Definition: (2k choose k) — drawing without replacement.

Term: How do you prove an interleaving is impossible?
Definition: Show what must happen before what; via transitivity you reach a contradiction (a cycle when drawn).

Term: What does parallel behaviour via shared memory depend on?
Definition: Hardware; runtime system; and programming language.

Term: Why can sequential code break when run in parallel?
Definition: Compiler; CPU and memory reorder instructions for performance; correct sequentially but may break under concurrency.

Term: Are modern architectures (x86; AMD64; ARM) sequentially consistent?
Definition: No — they are NOT sequentially consistent; reordering can occur.

Term: Two slow fixes for bugs from CPU memory reordering
Definition: synchronized (slow) and volatile (slow).

Term: What does the Java Memory Model (JMM) answer?
Definition: Which guarantees you have about the order of execution across threads.
Order of statements on a single thread in isolation; total order per thread but only partial order across threads.
Critical actions needing a fixed order: read/write of volatile; lock/unlock monitor; first/last/start/terminate action of a thread.
Global total order over all synchronization actions; every thread agrees on it; a volatile read/write makes prior updates visible.
Handshake where two threads touch the same sync action; a volatile write synchronizes-with every later volatile read of that variable.
Transitive closure of program order and synchronizes-with; everything A did before the handshake is visible to B.
It sees the most recent write in its HB chain; OR any unordered write (no HB relation).
It sees an outdated write (already overwritten in HB chain); OR a future write (one that happens-before the read).

Term: Three requirements of a critical section / lock
Definition: 1) Mutual exclusion; 2) Freedom from deadlock; 3) Freedom from starvation.

Term: Mutual exclusion in a state-space diagram
Definition: There is no state containing both p3 and q3 (both in critical section).

Term: No deadlock in a state-space diagram
Definition: There is no state without an outgoing arrow.

Term: No livelock in a state-space diagram
Definition: There is no infinite cycle that skips the critical section; from every node a path reaches the CS.
Every thread that wants the critical section eventually gets it.

Term: Memory needed to build a lock for n processes
Definition: At least n variables; O(n) memory.
volatile on an array only makes the pointer atomic; the elements are NOT volatile. Use AtomicIntegerArray.
Starvation-free.
Set flag = interested; mark myself victim so the other goes first; wait while other is interested; enter CS; clear flag.
Correct and fair (for 2 threads).
Extension of Peterson to n threads; each level uses Peterson with one victim; filters until one thread reaches the CS.
Mutual exclusion; deadlock-free; starvation-free; but NOT fair (no first-come-first-serve).
Waiting room with drawn tickets: take a number one higher than the max outstanding; enter when your ticket is lowest; thread-ID breaks ties. It is fair.
Test-and-Set (set 1 if currently 0); Compare-and-Swap (if memory == old; write new); Load-Linked/Store-Conditional (ARM).

Term: How does a TAS lock work?
Definition: Threads spin doing TAS in a while loop; only one gets old value 0 and enters; needs a single memory location.

Term: Problem with a plain TAS lock
Definition: All threads constantly spam TAS on the same location; heavy bus traffic; slow.
On failure sleep a random duration; double the expected wait each failure; reset once acquired; reduces simultaneous retries.
Test-and-Test-and-Set: first read the flag cheaply; only if it looks free attempt the TAS; else back off.
The directed graph of thread/lock wait relations has a cycle (A waits B; B waits C; C waits A).
get(); set(); compareAndSet(expect; update); getAndSet(newValue).

Term: Bank transfer: why not many small critical sections?
Definition: Money is briefly gone (non-atomic); breaks atomicity.

Term: Bank transfer: best solution to avoid deadlock
Definition: Global ordering of locks (e.g. by account number); the whole program must obey it to avoid cycles.
A counter for available slots; allows up to s threads in the CS (like a parking garage of capacity s).
acquire(S) decrements the counter (blocks at 0); release(S) increments it.
A lock allows 0 or 1 thread in the CS; a semaphore allows up to s threads.
Threads wait until all have reached a common point; only then may all continue.
acquire then immediately release; threads release each other one by one.

Term: Requirements for a correct reusable barrier
Definition: Protect count++ with a mutex; count must return to 0 at the end (reusable); only one thread triggers the release/acquire; not all at once.
Two turnstiles (barrier1; barrier2): phase 1 waits for all to arrive; phase 2 waits for all to leave; prevents a fast thread from lapping.
A linear array behaves circular: position mod length; index jumps from end back to start.

Term: Producer/Consumer: how to detect empty and full
Definition: Empty: in == out. Full: (in+1) % size == out — one slot is left unused so you need no counter variable.
Two counting semaphores (nonEmpty; nonFull) plus one binary semaphore (manipulation) protecting buf/in/out.
One lock protects the buffer; two conditions: producers await notFull; consumers await notEmpty.
Avoid signalling when nobody waits; barber checks waiting room and sleeps; client enqueues or wakes barber; use counters m (clients) and n (barbers).
m<=0: buffer full; -m clients waiting. n<=0: buffer empty; -n barbers waiting.
A generalization of Java's intrinsic (synchronized) locks; a data structure with wait / notify / notifyAll.
Threads trying to acquire the lock; one succeeds and becomes owner.
Threads that released the lock and sleep; woken by notify; then compete in the entry set again.
If all threads are in the waiting state; nobody can wake anyone.
Signaller keeps running; it just moves the signalled thread from wait set to entry set.
Signaller hands the lock to the signalled thread and goes to the entry queue.
On a manual Lock you create conditions (lock.newCondition()); still ONE lock but grouped wait sets; methods await() / signal() / signalAll().

Term: Why while(condition) wait() and not if?
Definition: After being woken and re-acquiring the lock the condition may be false again (another thread changed state); you must re-check in a loop.
notify() wakes an arbitrary single thread; it may be the wrong kind (e.g. a producer instead of a consumer) leading to lost wakeups/deadlock.
0 <= writers <= 1; 0 <= readers; writers * readers == 0 (never both).
A basic RW lock is unfair: if readers are much faster; writers may starve. Make fair with wait/notify and waiting-counters.
One lock for the whole structure (e.g. synchronized add/remove/contains). Simple but low concurrency.
Each list element has its own lock; more concurrency but more lock/unlock overhead.
Traverse holding two locks at a time; acquire the next before releasing the previous so no thread can overtake; lock both nodes you modify.
Traverse without locks; then lock only the needed nodes; then validate that nothing changed in between; retry if not.
Rescan from head to check pred is still reachable AND pred.next == curr (connection still intact).
Like optimistic but add a 'deleted' mark flag; logically delete by marking; physically unlink later; validate by checking marks + next pointer instead of rescanning.
Traverse while key < target; return true iff current key == target AND node is not marked (lock-free).
Always deadlock-free; failure of one thread cannot block another; but starvation is still possible.
Freedom from starvation; every thread finishes in finite steps. Wait-freedom implies lock-freedom.
If memory == old; set memory = new and return true (change made); else return false. Used for lock-free writes.
Read the shared variable into a local; prepare the change; use CAS to commit — if someone interleaved; retry the loop.
CAS assumes no write happened between read and swap; but another thread may change A->B->A; value looks equal though state changed.
Pointer tagging (use extra bits as a counter); hazard pointers.

Term: Lock-free linked list deletion needs what?
Definition: Atomic mark + unlink; AtomicMarkableReference (pointer + mark bit): getReference(); attemptMark(); compareAndSet on [ref; mark].
Two pointers (head; tail) plus a dummy sentinel node at the front to avoid null cases; enqueue/dequeue help advance tail (CAS).
Non-overlapping operations take effect in order; for overlapping operations nothing is guaranteed (could even swap within a thread).
Threads may interleave; but each thread's own order is preserved; you may move operations left/right without swapping; writes appear instantly visible.
Each operation takes effect at a single point between its invocation and return; if such points exist making everything correct; it is linearizable.
Linearizable => sequentially consistent. In linearizability you cannot move operation lines; you only pick the effect point within each line.
Valid (agreed value was proposed by someone); Consistent (all agree on the same value); Wait-free (returns in finite steps even if others halt).
Atomic read/write registers: 1. Test-and-Set: 2. Compare-and-Swap: n (any number).
Equivalent to general consensus; you can build each from the other using the ternary/boolean-to-int trick.

Currently bivalent but every next move makes it univalent; a bivalent state with two univalent children.
Every consensus protocol has a critical state; because you can only move down (wait-free; no loops) you must eventually reach a univalent state.

Term: Why can't atomic registers give wait-free consensus?
Definition: From a critical state whatever A reads/writes; B cannot tell it apart from executing directly; B would have to output two different values — contradiction; so registers have consensus number 1.
You declare 'atomic' blocks and don't manage the how; execution runs concurrently but appears sequential (serialized).
TM is atomic but NOT mutex; several threads may start a transaction at the same time.
As soon as an inconsistency between the local and shared version is detected the transaction aborts (not merely fails to commit).
Strong: safe even if a non-transactional thread accesses the variable. Weak: shared state may only be read/modified inside transactions.
Flat: one big transaction; inner failure aborts everything. Closed: inner transaction can abort and retry without aborting the outer.
Weak isolation and closed nesting; uses Callable when a return value is needed instead of Runnable.
Instead of aborting; wait until something changes and retry; no busy spin-wait.

Global clock (incremented via CAS); each transaction records a birthdate; keeps a read set and write set; on access use local copy if present else fetch and check the external timestamp is older; abort if newer; on commit lock; re-check; write back with updated birthdate.
Avoid shared state: each thread has private state; they cooperate only by sending messages (distributed memory).
A set of threads that can talk about a task; a thread can join several communicators; each has a rank (id) within each communicator.
All processes run the same program; branch on rank (e.g. rank 0 = master distributes work; else worker computes).
Synchronous: send then wait until the receiver actively receives. Asynchronous: send then continue immediately (needs a buffer).
Blocking: returns when the buffer is reusable (transfer may not be done). Non-blocking: returns immediately.

Term: MPI: how to avoid send/recv deadlock
Definition: Order operations carefully (one side Send then Recv; other Recv then Send); use Sendrecv; or use non-blocking Isend/Irecv + Waitall.
